title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
abstract: Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago. Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. OpenAI has taken several stumbles Image Credits: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg / Getty Images Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. Apple’s Siri AI Image Credits: Artur Widak/NurPhoto / Getty Images When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Character.ai Image Credits: Character.AI Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December. Relay Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. Ollie Image Credits: Ollie Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text. However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital. Microsoft’s Recall Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail Image Credits: Notion Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . Humane AI Pin Image Credits: Brian Heater The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention. But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million. Rabbit R1 Image Credits: Rabbit The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch. However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations. The company hasn’t given up, though.

title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
abstract: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters’ review of procurement notices, investment plans and corporate disclosures. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. Singapore In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. Japan In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
abstract: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
abstract: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely . But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere . This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair . Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube , where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder . Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth. What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years. Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff? Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment. The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way.

title: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
abstract: Tech AI Report Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.﻿ by Sean Hollister Nov 14, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at CES 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada, on January 6, 2025. | Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images Part Of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next? see all updates Sean Hollister is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget. On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights. Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs , including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump. The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company , he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down. The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job ; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100 , then carry on leading the company as a robot. It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO . “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli. “Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me. But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO. “He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me. Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil , leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs. Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off. I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new. But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them. His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot. What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets. In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024. He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC. Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit , he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent. “Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.” “NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla. “Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me. It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects , the company lost 80 percent of its market value. But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge. That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet , which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution. Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars , he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013, I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out.

title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
abstract: Tech AI News Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data Listing the details of everything for sale everywhere is meant to make Amazon more useful than Reddit for people and AI agents.﻿ Listing the details of everything for sale everywhere is meant to make Amazon more useful than Reddit for people and AI agents.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 13, 2026, 11:49 PM UTC Image: The Verge Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn’t sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters . The project, called the “World Product Graph,” is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they’re searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents — if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end up on its pages. Links to outside retailers’ products have already started popping up on Amazon through the “shop direct” feature it launched last year. The company also has its own AI shopping assistant , Alexa for Shopping, previously called Rufus. The World Product Graph project would also be aimed at fixing issues with the AI by providing it more data. According to Reuters , an internal Amazon document on the project says “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete” and running users’ Amazon searches with the AI is expensive. Adding more data is reportedly supposed to make the system more accurate and able to use cheaper models. Whether this actually ships is still up in the air. The internal document reportedly says the project “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” which could involve Amazon crawling other retailers’ sites. Reuters says it’s unclear “if or when this plan may be implemented,” but said the document on it included an October 1st, 2027 release date. Amazon said in a statement to Reuters that “Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy
abstract: Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp , a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy . Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace , an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out. It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull: The research post frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly. The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking: The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability. dspy-wsp turns that research loop into a standard DSPy optimizer. The GitHub Repo describes 3 actors: The writer works in turns. Each turn has a short explanation, then 1 code block. That block is either: Forward passes come from a fixed budget ( max_passes=25 in the tests). When the budget runs out, the writer’s best edit becomes the patch. A hidden validation set then compares original and edited weights on the same examples and seeds. The repo is explicit about data separation: The results write-up lists every edit. The edits are small and targeted: d1-2B has no decision head, so the writer edited its backbone at layer 23. On d1-omni-600M, the writer rewrote part of the decision head’s scorer. The Repo example triages support tickets. The signature uses only decision-type outputs: After compile , the program calls the edited local model instead of a hosted API. compiled.wsp_patch.summary() shows what changed. Cmpnd tested on Typed Decisions , a benchmark for typed probabilistic decisions. A model reads 1 piece of unstructured state and answers 5 typed questions at once. Each answer is a probability distribution. The test split has 400 cases and 2,000 decisions. Each model got 25 forward passes from GPT-6-Astra. Gains are paired, with a standard error of ±0.7 to 1.4 points. Sources: Cmpnd blog chart for d1-omni-600M, d1-2B and Clef-Flash; results README for NanoJev. ReAnchor is an earlier Cmpnd optimizer. Decision models output probabilities, and thresholds turn those into answers. ReAnchor refits each question’s thresholds with no LLM calls. WeightSpace changes the model; ReAnchor recalibrates its output. The 2 stack well. The answer is yes. With gpt-6.1-sol as the writer, WeightSpace alone gave +5.8 on d1-omni-600M, +12.1 on NanoJev and −0.6 on d1-2B. Astra produced +16.1, +13.3 and +13.4 on the same models. Slightly, and Cmpnd says so. By default, the writer can recompute the decision head inside its kernel. Setting simulate_head=False enforces the paper’s stricter rule. Under that rule, d1-omni-600M gained only +2.8 ± 0.7 points. Adding ReAnchor brought it to +9.3, no better than ReAnchor alone. Each run writes a patch to run_dir . The patch holds manifest.json and edit.npz , with only the changed entries. It also stores sha256 hashes of every base and edited tensor. Anyone with the public base model can rebuild the edited weights exactly. The edited model runs locally. On Apple silicon it uses MLX. On Linux it uses PyTorch, on an NVIDIA GPU if present. Text-generating LLMs work through VLLMBackend (NVIDIA), HFBackend (CUDA, MPS or CPU) and MLXBackend (Apple silicon). A GEPASearch option, contributed by Michael Isaac, adds population search for decision models. Check out the Cmpnd blog post , the GitHub repo , the full results and the original Weight-Space Programming research . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: Stanford Research Open-Sources Memorilla, a Latent Memory Module for Frozen LLMs
abstract: Stanford researchers have released Memorilla , an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context . It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0 . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT. A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store. Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs. All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team. Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there. Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success. On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms. An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile , the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents. Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained . The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B as Stage 1, 2, 3, PV4 and PMv2 folders. Each checkpoint must run with the decoder it was trained with ( evaluation docs ). Custom data needs parquet files with collection_id , question , answer and documents columns. The research team also released PersonalizationV4 : 149 synthetic users, 200 conversations each, under CC BY 4.0. Benchmark scores come from Memorilla’s paper, which ran every baseline on the same Qwen3-8B. Licenses come from each project’s repository. Check out the paper , browse the GitHub repo , and download the checkpoints . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: Vercel Releases UI SDK: 50+ UI Behaviors for AI Coding Agents
abstract: Vercel Labs has released UI SDK , an open-source beta library of interface behaviors built for coding agents. Vercel UI SDK is a headless library that ships behaviors, not finished components. Agents combine those behaviors into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . UI SDK is a library of UI behaviors from Vercel Labs that agents assemble into components. The README lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop, and the ARIA they need. All of it lives in @ui-sdk/core . Thin adapters render it in each framework. The project site explains the idea with a Select. You do not hand the agent a finished Select. You hand it a popup, a selection model and typeahead. Those same parts can produce an autocomplete, a combobox, or a component nobody has designed yet. Components start as primitives defined with definePrimitive . A primitive declares state, an API and slots. Slots attach attributes, events and behaviors to DOM parts. The README example builds a search field with createFocusRecovery . Its Clear button appears only when there is text. Each framework then renders the primitive with createParts . The README says the parts are the same in all 5 adapters. So 1 behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app. Behaviors shown on ui-sdk.dev include: The docs group behaviors into 10 categories, from Focus and Keys to Canvas. Prebuilt components include Select, Combobox, Date Picker, Menu, Tree and Color Picker. Setup is a prompt you paste into your agent . It installs the packages and adds a note to AGENTS.md . That note points the agent to the ui-sdk skill and to llms.txt inside the package docs. The skill installs with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk . Pages without a build step can load web.js and web.css from ui-sdk.dev, per the skill listing . Yes, the agent docs describe a bridge created with createAgent() before the page renders. agent.snapshot() lists components, their state and available actions. agent.act() runs an action, such as renaming a project with setValue . Apps can pass an allow callback to approve or refuse actions. Change callbacks receive source: "agent" and can cancel the change. Tools can also be registered with supported browsers through WebMCP. Vercel compared its bridge against browser tools on 1 project-settings task. The agent renamed a project, updated members and notification settings, then saved. Both agents used Sonnet through Claude Code, with the same task and system prompt. Figures are medians of 3 runs . Treat these as directional. The sample is 1 task, and the browser-tools run used a different component library. Vercel does not name the Sonnet version. All 6 packages are on npm at 0.1.0-beta.1 , published November 12, 2026, under Apache-2.0. Install with npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core , swapping the adapter per framework. Peer requirements are strict: React 19+ , Vue 3.5+ , Svelte 5.33+ and Solid 2.0.0-rc.14+ . An optional web.css file gives components a default look. Versions and peer ranges are from npm as of November 13, 2026. React Aria hooks and Ark UI’s Zag.js machines already separate behavior from markup. UI SDK’s difference is the agent layer: a skill, bundled llms.txt and a runtime bridge Check out the GitHub repo , docs and npm package . title: Production MLOps at GS Caltex with Amazon SageMaker Canvas, part 1
abstract: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. The following diagram shows how process engineers hand off SageMaker Canvas assets to ML engineers for deployment and scheduled inference. ML engineers use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for preprocessing flows and Model Registry for model versions, then schedule pipeline runs through Amazon EventBridge. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. After that review, they approve the model in Model Registry and deploy it. This preparation takes place when a new model version is deployed. Subsequent inference runs reuse the deployed model. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform , and stores the results in S3. ML engineers can inspect step status and Amazon CloudWatch logs to monitor the workflow. The production pipeline reuses the preprocessing logic and trained model created in SageMaker Canvas. ML engineers configure the input and output paths, set the order of execution, and write the code that connects approval and scheduling to the workflow. Before you begin, prepare the following: The full reference implementation is available in the GitHub repository . The code examples in this post focus on the connections between components. The repository uses a sample loan classification model, so adjust the configuration to match your model’s input and output formats. The following steps cover preprocessing reuse, model approval and deployment, pipeline construction, and scheduled inference. A preprocessing flow created with Data Wrangler in SageMaker Canvas records the data sources and transformation steps. To set up the reference implementation, export data to Amazon S3 using SageMaker Processing, then retrieve the job settings and the .flow file used by that job. In the export settings, turn off Auto job configuration and select SageMaker Processing . After the export starts, open the Processing job details on the Amazon SageMaker AI console. Record the container image URI, the S3 URI of the input named flow , the execution role, and the output settings. Use these values to configure the pipeline step that runs the .flow file. The SageMaker execution role must have permissions to read the required S3 data, write the results, and access the container image. Choose the instance type and count based on the volume of data you need to process. Keep the preprocessing logic validated by the process engineer, and adjust the data sources, paths, and other settings for the production environment. Check the container image and output node against the original job configuration. Some .flow files contain execution metadata such as internal_metadata.dw_job.container_uri . Check the actual Processing job settings rather than assuming that every export contains this field. If you move the workflow to another AWS Region, verify that the container image is available there. The reference implementation separates intermediate and final outputs by execution under runs/<execution-id>/ . Its PrepareInput step writes data to a fixed S3 location referenced by the .flow file. Prevent executions that share that input path from overlapping. To isolate input data for each execution as well, add a preparation step that updates the source URI in a copy of the .flow file. Declaring a SageMaker Pipelines parameter does not automatically replace a URI inside the file. The target column is one difference between training and inference data. A flow built with training data can contain transformations that expect the target column in the input schema. Inference data does not contain that known outcome. The reference implementation adds a PrepareInput step before preprocessing. If the target column is missing, this step adds it with a placeholder value. After preprocessing, DropTargetColumn removes the column. Match the placeholder’s data type and column position to the training schema, and pass only the expected features to the model in their original order. Use this approach only when the placeholder target does not affect feature values. A flow that filters rows by the target, derives features from it, or applies target encoding needs additional treatment. In those cases, separate the transformations and learned state required for inference. Validation should cover column order and count, data types, missing-value handling, and row count. After removing the target, check that the remaining columns match the feature order used during training. Register the validated SageMaker Canvas model version in Model Registry . The registered version can include the model files, inference configuration, and evaluation results. ML engineers review this information before changing the approval status. The model file, such as model.tar.gz , must be used with the correct inference container and environment settings. A model package in Model Registry groups this information together. In this batch architecture, deployment creates a SageMaker model resource from an approved package for Batch Transform to reference. The following example checks a package that has already been approved, then creates the model resource. Supply model_package_arn , model_name , and sagemaker_role_arn during deployment. This example uses a unique model name for each version. Model Registry records approval status, but it does not enforce an approval check on every inference request. Check that status in the deployment code and retain the selected package ARN and model name in the pipeline configuration. If approval is revoked, update the schedules and execution configurations that use the model. Registration and deployment take place when a model version is released.

title: Open-source AI without Jensen
abstract: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out. Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models. There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety” . Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting. Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work. As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king. The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen. The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis emergency podcast : Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it. Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot? No. Moonshot skill-wise is probably just as good as the US labs. They just have a big deficit in compute and deployment. So I think if we don’t have a scale advantage, then you don’t win. Yes, these smaller labs have spent a lot of money on models. But DeepMind, Grok, Meta have regularly fallen behind the frontier of Chinese labs, and they’re spending more. So it’s not just, oh, spend a few billion dollars and you can make a model that’s better. The best people for attracting talent are the ones at the front of movements. Jensen helped catalyze this, and on many metrics was still losing. Nemotron has had the right level of ambition and strong people, but it hasn’t delivered to the point of being called “mission accomplished.” The competition here in building leading-edge models is more fierce than most give credit to. Having an organization with billions of dollars, solid people, and good vibes may not get you there. You normally need something special. It could be the case that Thinking Machines has gotten to maturity in its commitment to open models, with its recent Inkling 2 Small being the best Western open-weight model in a while. Still, it’s far behind Kimi K3.1 Pro and expectations are high for Zhipu’s next GLM update. It’s a better sign that we’re at least having this debate, but the open ecosystem is riddled with questions and answers like this – maybe they can pull it off? On the other side of the equation, closed labs like Anthropic look like some of the greatest businesses ever assembled, which inspires confidence in the longevity of their approach. Who is Mira going to call when they need to close their next funding round? Supposedly the next round at a $40B valuation is a done deal, but that won’t be enough to keep pace with the closed frontier for long. The fundamental problem is that the open-weight ecosystem needs someone who will pick up the phone to abate a crisis. There are more challenges ahead. The most likely allies we could turn to are from the hyperscalers, the likes of Zuckerberg, Andy Jassy, or Satya. With such a coordinated campaign of pressure from the AI safety community that has open models as a negative target, I worry that being proactive is the only way to stay ahead.

title: 輝達上演“奧特曼2.0”，員工集體請願：讓老黃回家！
abstract: 輝達上演“奧特曼2.0”，員工集體請願：讓老黃回家！ 鷺羽 2026-11-14 18:08:08 來源： 量子位 馬斯克也簽名了 鷺羽 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 嚯！輝達極速上演「奧特曼」宮鬥2.0—— 員工集體聯名上書 ，要求老黃迴歸！ 連馬斯克都簽了。。。 一份要求恢復老黃職位的請願正在進行中，家人們我已衝。 不愧是好兄弟哇！危難時方顯義薄雲天（bushi） 不過董事會未必如願。 有訊息稱，輝達董事會已秘密接觸 Arm執行長 Rene Haas，考慮作為黃仁勳的潛在繼任者。 而Haas早年就在輝達擔任高管。 董事會VS員工，喬幫主還是奧特曼，黃仁勳正站在風口浪尖。 “回來吧，老黃！” 一石激起千層浪。 對黃仁勳的聲援，已經從公司內部蔓延至整個矽谷。 其支持者也公開發起了 “33 Years Deserve an Answer” （33年，值得一個交代）的獨立請願活動，呼籲讓老黃重返CEO崗位。 目前已有6萬多人簽署，而且該資料還在持續暴漲。 其中不乏輝達的前任和現任員工、合作夥伴及股東。 比如 馬斯克 。 請願訴求主要有三點： 1、在獨立調查完成、相關事實得到確認之前， 恢復黃仁勳的CEO職務 。 2、 公開調查框架與時間安排 ，保障黃仁勳的申辯權利。 3、向員工及股東充分 解釋董事會決策依據 。 這也是絕大多數內部員工的意見。 據WIRED報道，一則要求董事會考慮員工意見的內部建議帖，已經積累了 超過1600條評論 ，其中多數支援黃仁勳迴歸。 該帖由一名資深工程師在黃仁勳辭職前發出。 結果當地時間11月12日，輝達突然宣佈，黃仁勳辭去總裁、CEO和董事職務，立即生效。 長期擔任CFO的 Colette Kress 接任臨時CEO，公司同時開始尋找正式繼任者。 隨後，更多員工湧入該貼，留言呼籲 “把老闆請回來” 。 還有人發出全員郵件，要求公司更透明地解釋黃仁勳離職的全過程。 我挺老黃！人非聖賢，孰能無過？講道理，總不至於要把這位帶著我們一路走來的老大“一鍵拉黑”吧？ 更有甚者直接表示： 輝達之所以成為輝達，全靠黃仁勳。 你別說，這話還真沒毛病。 輝達的組織架構有多逆天呢？幾十位相關負責人直接向他彙報。 最多的時候，老黃的直接下屬 超過60人 ，覆蓋記憶體、CPU、GPU、架構和演算法等各個方向。 對內如此，對外也是有求必應。 初創公司exolabs創始人Alex Cheema，就分享了他被老黃行動力驚到的經歷。 今年6月，團隊成員給黃仁勳發了一封郵件，提出一個大膽的想法： 把輝達硬體上的本地AI效能提升到原來的10倍。 結果，郵件發出 僅7分鐘 ，老黃就親自回覆，還直接批准團隊在輝達總部設立專門的專案作戰室。 不僅如此，輝達還安排了密集的技術交流。CUDA、Dynamo的開發者，以及參與輝達早期建設的工程師，都主動提出幫助，最終合作實現9.6倍的效能加速。 老實說，這樣敢為小公司下注的CEO，恐怕再難找到第二個。 輝達如今能一躍成為行業龍頭，也離不開老黃十年如一日的 CUDA 堅守。 早年應用寥寥、投入遲遲難見回報，他頂著質疑，帶著團隊把GPU一步步帶向AI時代，才有輝達今天在AI算力領域的地位。 老黃早已不僅是輝達的CEO，說是技術風向標、靈魂人物也不為過。 喬布斯之於蘋果，黃仁勳之於輝達。 接班傳聞指向Arm掌門人 但董事會顯然不這麼想。 斷尾求生也好，緩兵之計也罷，董事會已然開始尋找 “下一個黃仁勳” 。 《金融時報》報道稱，輝達董事會在尋找黃仁勳的潛在繼任者時，接觸了Arm CEO Rene Haas 。 這並非空穴來風。 Haas在2006年出任輝達計算產品業務部門副總裁兼總經理，2013年轉入Arm，之後歷任戰略聯盟、商務及IP產品業務等管理崗位，於2022年成為Arm CEO。 換句話說，他既有輝達的底子，又有管理另一家重要晶片技術公司的經驗。 對於一家突然失去長期掌舵者的企業來說，這樣的履歷的確夠亮眼。 不過輝達隨後表示： 公司仍在選擇協助尋找繼任者的獵頭機構，對具體候選人的猜測目前都 “為時過早” 。 那…不妨給蘇媽一個機會？還都是親戚（doge） 說正經的，業內還是更普遍傾向於 Colette Kress 和 Ian Buck 。 前者長期負責公司財務，已被正式任命為臨時CEO；後者參與了CUDA軟體體系的發展，並負責公司的超大規模AI相關產品業務。 都是公司老員工了，也更熟悉輝達的日常運轉。 至於老黃何去何從，還是個未解之謎。 或許可以去找奧特曼取取經，又或者接下馬斯克的橄欖枝： One More Thing 外界紛紛擾擾，結果你猜老黃在幹嘛？ 外媒扒了扒—— 此刻的老黃，正坐在自己價值3800萬美元的舊金山豪宅裡。 和親友嗨皮， 吃炸雞、恰薯條 。 亂成一鍋了，趁熱吃吧。 參考連結： [1] title: 「史上最嚴」溼實驗預測基準釋出！推理拉滿、算力翻5倍也白搭
abstract: 「史上最嚴」溼實驗預測基準釋出！推理拉滿、算力翻5倍也白搭 鷺羽 2026-11-14 17:58:22 來源： 量子位 斯坦福、哈佛、康奈爾……十餘家頂尖團隊齊坐一桌了 鷺羽 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 不ber，現在的基準測試都進化到醬嬸了？？？ 這回不刷題了，就直接給AI一組實驗條件，讓它 自己研究、提前猜真實溼實驗的結果 …… 比如，同一個反應換幾種條件，哪種能得到更多目標產物？一批抗體變體，哪個表達量更高？ 答案先藏好，等AI交卷，再拿實測結果對一對。 你還別說，這事兒現在真值得一測。 這兩年， AI for Science 的方式越來越深入，AI已經能自主查文獻、用軟體，為完成一項分析任務連續做上幾小時也不在話下。 大家自然而然開始進入下一個階段： 我們到底希望AI具備怎樣的科研能力？ 溼實驗結果預測 ，就是其中頗有實際價值的一項。 它需要AI理解實驗目標，並從已有知識中挖掘出相關機制，才能更好地幫助研究人員篩選值得進一步探索的研究方向。 UniPat AI牽頭推出的新基準 Science Prediction Universe （簡稱SPU），便敏銳地察覺到這一點。 116個任務，4207個溼實驗，覆蓋化學、材料科學、生物和醫學，基準顧問與溼實驗合作成員也來自斯坦福、康奈爾、哈佛等高校，以及業內前沿科研機構和生物技術公司。 模型踐行每次工作8小時制，配有一塊H20，然後自主決定怎樣利用檢索與計算資源形成實驗預測。 結果出乎所有人意料。 即使強如Opus 5.5、GPT-6 Astra，資料上 距離真正能實現預測還都很遙遠 。。。 各配置在全部已評分任務上的平均得分 不得不說，SPU這是給所有科研模型都上了道硬菜。 從前那些看不見摸不著的科研能力，如今都變成了可以統一評估、持續研究的數值。 至於AI的科研判斷怎樣一步步養成，就有了更為具體的討論依據。 溼實驗預測：值得單獨為模型考一次 回到 溼實驗預測 上，首先這的確不是一道新題。 科學史上有過很多這樣的時刻，一個判斷在實驗之前被給出，然後交給過程去裁決，對了就留下，錯了就推翻。 具體的判斷邏輯就構成了科學家的 品味 。 品味夠好、直覺夠準，科學家就能更快拿到大結果，同時節省寶貴的實驗資源。 畢竟光一次溼實驗，做化學的要配試劑、設定反應條件，再分離產物；做生物的也要經過漫長的蛋白表達……時間成本、工具費用本身就價格不菲，結果不理想還得反反覆覆做好幾輪。 所以 在動手之前先預測 ，是科研流程裡含金量最高的一步。 只不過區別在於，過去這件事純靠科學家自己，現在到了AI時代，模型也需要有這項能力，並且還需要一張能為之打分的試卷。 現有的基準還無法完全覆蓋 ，比如BrainBench讓模型直接判斷實驗結果，ScienceAgentBench側重在已有資料上完成分析，Terminal-Bench 4.0和Long-Horizon-TB這類長程任務基準，則主要用預設測試檢查任務產物。 SPU與之相比，均有所不同。 它更強調把AI自主研究過程與溼實驗結果預測放在一起考， 既涉及預測效果，也考驗科學工具使用和長程任務執行的能力 。 圖表由AI生成 這種判斷也被SPU組織成了明確的任務。 100個公開任務 分別取自85篇近期釋出的論文，領域專家從研究中整理候選項、材料、條件與測量方式，保留完整的定量結果作為評分依據。 另外 16個私有任務 ，來自四組未發表的合作溼實驗，涉及VHH奈米抗體、反應條件、電解液和Magrolimab變體。 共計32個子領域、4207個實驗，其中公開研究提供了跨學科的任務來源， 實測結果對模型隱藏 ，未發表實驗則增加了獨立於公開論文答案的檢驗。 這在一定程度上可以避免模型提前見過題目。 SPU的任務覆蓋與來源 題目的篩選過程也很有講究。 專家優先選擇測量完整、條件清楚的研究，那些沿著單一趨勢就能排序的簡單問題會被直接剔除，數值過於接近的問題也會被視作參考意義不大。 最終留下來的那些題，都會更難也更有區分度。 具體預測過程中，要求模型 每次執行八小時 ，配8核CPU、16 GiB記憶體和一塊H20，同時允許聯網檢索並安裝科研軟體。 模型將在這段時間裡自行蒐集證據、選擇計算方法，最後提交各比較組 從低到高的預測排序 。 為了防止記憶汙染，評分過程也會全程在獨立、斷網的容器中進行，禁止AI檢索原始研究結果，還會自動掃描工具輸出，識別源論文DOI、標題等識別符號。 最後系統將用 Spearman相關係數 對照預測與實測排序。 係數越接近1，排序就越貼近實驗結果。 SPU的評測流程 有意思的是，SPU還關注到了很多基準測試沒有考慮到的細節。 比如對於最後的得分，SPU會考慮會不會是運氣使然，萬一是瞎貓碰到死耗子了呢。 所以它會額外為每道題生成4000份隨機排序，把第95百分位作為隨機水平閾值，檢查模型提交是否明顯超過這一參照。不同任務也都有相應的參照依據。 整套SPU的設計，可以說是科學嚴謹的。 模型要在裡面一步步自己判斷什麼值得算，併為最終預測交卷。 這一設計既有利於衡量當前AI的溼實驗預測能力，也為後續研究團隊藉助統一指標持續改進實驗指明瞭方向。 說歸說，咱們接下來不妨一起看看首批前沿模型的成績單。箇中細節還挺值得單獨拎出來講講。 全新測試讓前沿模型集體破繃 SPU首輪系統評測覆蓋 12款前沿模型、13種配置 。這裡的配置，指的是模型、推理強度以及所使用的模型框架。 先說說整體成績。 一句話： 都不咋地。 在全部已評分任務上，平均分最高的是Claude Opus 5.5，拿了0.486分。但其中也只有一半的任務，超過了隨機水平。 13個配置裡，幾乎都是這樣，能超過隨機水平閾值的任務比例僅有 34％～52％ 。 也就是說，在場的所有模型距離真正可靠的溼實驗預測，都還有一段很長的距離。 領先組和落後組的行為對比分析 不過模型之間亦有差距，平均表現可以劃分為兩個梯隊： 領先組 （6個模型）和 落後組 （7個模型）。 同題比較中，領先組平均還是要比其餘七個高出約 0.15分 。 還有個細節值得注意。領先組約9％的任務得分低於0，其餘七個配置的這一比例能高達22％。 這裡的0指的就是隨機有效排序的平均分，負分即意味著預測與實際排序呈負相關。 差距具體來自哪兒呢？研究團隊又往下深挖了一步。 他們先把同題中其它模型的預測合成一份 參考排序 ，再將實驗兩兩配對，對照實測結果，檢查每個模型單獨有沒有排對。 在參考排序正確的實驗對上，領先組能排對 86％ ，其餘七個配置為78％；而對於參考排序錯誤的實驗對，兩組獨立排對的比例都在30％左右。 所以其實領先組的一部分優勢，恰恰體現在共同預測正確的地方，這部分領先組始終會更穩。 至於模型為什麼會偏離正確判斷，執行記錄裡有更具體的線索。 以 溶液任務 為例，同一個聚合反應，依次更換12種溶劑，任務要求按最後分離得到的聚合物質量排序。 Opus 5.5得分0.874，Qwen3.8為-0.126。12個候選溶劑條件兩兩配對，共66對，前者排對56對，後者排對30對。 同一道任務上Opus和Qwen的兩次執行 分析發現，這是因為 二者從一開始關注的因素就有所差別 ： Qwen3.8主要依據溶劑能溶解多少乙烯來排序，Opus 5.5更關注原料的混溶情況以及催化劑在溶劑中的相容性。 雖然Qwen3.8在計算過程中，也同樣發現了這一問題，但最終沒能直接改變模型最後採用的排序依據。 所以預測出錯最有可能發生的階段，就是在 選擇判斷依據 的那一步上，模型還要學會根據線索即時調整排序方式，才能讓這些發現真正影響答案。 拆開來看， 這些差異也會隨著具體學科與任務發生變化 。 在公開任務各學科的已評分結果中，化學平均分最高的是Opus 5.5，材料科學是Fable 5.1，生物學是GPT-6 Astra Medium，醫學是Opus 5。 P.S.Fable 5.1、Opus 5.5存在拒答現象。 各模型在四個學科上的得分 所以如果準備讓AI參與某一類研究，不妨先找個相關任務，拿來SPU測測，確定模型真的適用後再進行正式實驗。 私有任務的結果，把這一點講得更具體。 13個配置中有12個的平均分顯著高於隨機排序，配置之間沒有檢出明顯差異。相比之下， 不同任務帶來的變化 尤為醒目。 同一批電解液，預測離子電導率時，13個配置的排序相關係數集中在0.89～0.95；換成電化學視窗，12個獲評分配置的得分為-0.55～0.07，均未超過隨機水平閾值。 模型沒變，測量目標一換，成績分佈就明顯換了。 所以下次再評價一個模型時，只說它擅長化學還不夠具體，還要看它 具體面對哪一種測量目標、哪些實驗條件 。 各模型在16個私有任務上的預測表現 再講一個挺反直覺的事兒： 一般來說， 多給模型一些時間、更高的推理強度 ，成績應該會繼續往上走吧？ 大家普遍都是這樣想的，也都是這樣做的。 結果你猜咋地，SPU的結果一齣，直接啪啪打臉—— 在同樣的8小時運算下，研究團隊將GPT-6 Astra從中等推理強度調到最高，最高強度的執行時間中位數增至4.8倍，API成本中位數也增至5.3倍。 但預測得分…… 幾乎紋絲不動 。 嗯？研究團隊還特地回去翻了翻模型執行記錄。 結果好傢伙，在完成的79個任務上，GPT-6 Astra最高推理強度通常在執行到中位26％時，就已經給出了答案。 模型後續也沒閒著，繼續計算修改，但都是微調，沒能在結果中顯現出差異。 換言之， 推理強度再高，也不一定讓結果更好 。 GPT-6 Astra在兩種推理強度下的投入與表現 這個現象倒也給模型的資源分配提了個醒，如果要追加計算，千萬別盲目衝，耗時耗力還未必討巧。 相反可以 更細緻地沿著執行記錄檢查 ，先充分了解新增的證據究竟對應哪項判斷，再有目的性地局部提升算力。 其實在 工具使用 上，也有類似的現象顯現。 GPT-6 Astra Max每次執行使用的方法類別中位數為4類，Medium為1類，但兩種配置的得分仍未檢出顯著差別。 理由也差不多，都是好工具沒有用在刀刃上。 比如蒙特卡洛取樣，雖然大部分時間模型都在呼叫該工具，但只是給最後的排序加了點誤差範圍，沒有直接影響到結果本身。 科學計算工具呼叫情況 所以其實，工具用得再多也不如用得準。 GPU的使用情況 也提供了一個有意思的視角。 在提供了充足的GPU算力情況下，真正成功執行GPU計算的只有255次， 不到五分之一 。 不同模型、不同學科，跑GPU的情況也各不相同，所以單純看呼叫GPU的次數，本身很難說明模型科研能力。 要判斷算力有沒有幫上忙，還得看它被用來算了什麼、計算結果是否有助於預測，以及這些結果如何影響最終排序。 關鍵還是要將算力引到排序相關的 物理量 上，才能讓模型更為精準地完成預測。 GPU使用統計 搭配成本一起看，各配置每次執行的平均API成本，從0.22美元到65.91美元不等，差距足足 300倍 。 這意味著SPU同時提供預測表現與呼叫成本， 對準備部署科研模型的團隊，是個不錯的參考依據 。 從整體得分到同題軌跡 ，SPU把模型差異展開到了科研判斷的每一處細節裡，比如算力、比如成本。 AI算出的數值，對預測到底有多大幫助；預測出了錯，又該回頭檢查哪些判斷……這些都能結合實驗結果與執行記錄繼續分析。 下一輪改進也就有了可以明確嘗試的方向： 根據SPU， 模型能夠更及時發現錯誤假設，更有依據地保留或修改排序 。改完後，再放回相同任務，看看預測有沒有更準。 把「檢驗理解」搬進模型的考場 可以說， SPU與AI4S的發展規律高度契合 。 AI4S的評測正在逐步深入真實實驗環節，面向實驗執行的基準也在今年陸續出現。 但在執行之外， 預測 作為科研流程中繞不開的一步，也是最難量化的一步，終於有了可衡量的方式。 這樣的好處體現在兩方面： 研究者 由此可以分析，哪些測量目標更容易預測，哪些任務差異最大，以及一次錯誤判斷如何形成。既能節約昂貴且寶貴的實驗資源，也能縮短決策時間。 對 模型開發 而言，這也提供了更為具體的改進參照。 隨著實驗型別增多，評測也能回答更具體的問題：面對哪些材料、實驗條件和測量方式，AI給出的排序更可靠、更值得參考。 科學家由此可以圍繞同一類問題持續積累進展。 事實上，SPU還只是UniPat AI系列真實工作評測中的冰山一角： ScienceVision：關注模型如何從三維科學物件中獲取證據並回答問題； PaperBenchX：把已發表研究轉為可執行、可驗證的論文復現任務； SaaS-Bench及EvoCode-Bench：分別考察實際軟體流程與需求持續變化時的開發工作。 …… 這些工作覆蓋科研、辦公與軟體開發，共同關心AI進入具體工作後怎樣完成任務，以及結果如何得到驗證。 這也側面體現了，UniPat AI對AI走向科研實踐、甚至走向真實世界，擁有獨到的行業認知和前瞻性判斷。 UniPat AI也展示出一種新型的AI合作模式： 領域專家 參與任務篩選與稽核， 合作實驗室 提供未發表任務， 專案團隊 將不同學科的實驗組織成統一評測任務。 以SPU為例，由UniPat AI牽頭，顧問成員所屬機構包括斯坦福、康奈爾、哈佛、UIC、北大、港科大和FutureHouse。來自優睿賽思、愛博泰克、深度原理與恩和生物的溼實驗合作成員，參與了相關實驗工作。 跨學科知識與實驗資源由此進入同一套評測過程。SPU既承載了 對問題的選擇 ，也呈現出將科研問題組織成可執行任務所需的 協作 。 目前SPU相關的100個公開任務計劃以完整的Harbor任務包形式釋出；16個私有任務繼續保持私有，用於受控評測。資料集和程式碼都已經開源。 誠然，今天的AI，在這套SPU機制面前還只是新手。 它能把工具用得飛快，能在8小時裡裝三套軟體、跑完DFT再做蒙特卡洛，但在最關鍵的判斷上，它還沒學會問自己一句， 我算的這個量，是不是實驗真正需要測的那個量 。 但隨著這類任務持續積累，AI能夠承擔怎樣的科研工作，也將變得清晰。 SPU把這段距離量了出來，接下來每一次考試，都是AI向真實實驗臺走近的記錄。 專案主頁：https://spu.unipat.ai 論文連結： https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15049 GitHub開源連結： https://github.com/UniPat-AI/SPU
