title: DeepSeek Ultrafast
abstract:
DeepSeek Ultrafast An ultra-fast inference engine for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for sm_100a and sm_103a . It supports 1M context length and multi-server KV cache sharing. Performance 4 x GB300 (TP4) 8 x B300 (TP8) Decode (coding) 1,740 tokens/s 2,060 tokens/s Step time 3.30 ms 2.71 ms Acceptance length 5.6 tokens/step Prefill 1,000,000 tokens in 13.2 s (76,000 tokens/s) 1,000,000 tokens in 11.7 s (85,000 tokens/s) Decode, step time and acceptance length are measured on "implement the tetris game. output HTML code directly - no explanation." Each decode step drafts a block of tokens and verifies it; the acceptance length is the average number of tokens a step emits. Instructions for reproducing the results are at the bottom of this page. Streaming a complete Tetris game, with live decode speed, then playing it. Shown at real-time speed. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-Fast is available on Baseten Model APIs . More performance improvements and open source releases are coming. Quickstart Requirements 4 GB300 ( sm_103a ), 4 or 8 B300 ( sm_103a ) or 4 or 8 B200 ( sm_100a ) GPUs The CUDA 13 toolkit DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in models/ A Redis instance for multi-server KV cache coordination sudo apt-get install -y build-essential pkg-config cmake clang libclang-dev \ libibverbs-dev librdmacm-dev libopencv-dev redis-server curl ca-certificates
curl -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain none && . " $HOME /.cargo/env " 1. Build rustup toolchain install
DSUF_SM=sm_103a cargo build --release -p deepseek-ultrafast-engine --bin run -p deepseek-ultrafast-server --bin serve 2. Start a local server The server keeps each conversation's KV cache between turns. Redis records which replica owns
each conversation's cache; locally it only needs to be running. The server finds the machine's
RDMA ports itself: redis-server --bind 127.0.0.1 --save ' ' --appendonly no --daemonize yes DSUF_REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6379 target/release/serve --ckpt models --gpus 0,1,2,3 --port 8000 On an 8-GPU B300 machine, use all eight ( --gpus 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ; build with DSUF_SM=sm_103a ). It is ready when curl localhost:8000/readyz returns 200, about 20 seconds after start. 3. Connect your harness Use your favorite OpenAI-compatible client. For example: DEEPSEEK_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000 DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=none \ npx @deepseek-ai/dsh headless " summarize this repo " KV cache sharing in multi-server setups Every server keeps recent conversations' KV caches in host memory. When a conversation's next turn
lands on a different server, that server fetches the cache directly from the server that holds it,
host memory to host memory over RDMA, instead of recomputing the prompt. Redis records which server
owns each conversation's cache and announces ownership changes. Thanks to DeepSeek's extreme KV cache compression, the transfers are very fast and can be done on every request. This setup removes the need for prefix-aware routing and enables better load balancing. See deploy/kubernetes.yaml for an example multi-server deployment. Reproduce the demo Stream the Tetris answer from the server and report the decode speed: python3 - << ' EOF ' import json, time, urllib.request body = { "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "implement the tetris game. output HTML code directly - no explanation."}], "thinking": {"type": "disabled"}, "stream": True, "stream_options": {"include_usage": True}, } req = urllib.request.Request("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions", json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"}) start, first, tokens = time.time(), None, 0 with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as stream: for line in stream: if not line.startswith(b"data: {"): continue chunk = json.loads(line[6:]) if chunk.get("usage"): tokens = chunk["usage"]["completion_tokens"] for choice in chunk["choices"]: if text := choice["delta"].get("content"): first = first or time.time() print(text, end="", flush=True) end = time.time() print(f"\n\n{tokens} tokens at {tokens / (end - first):,.0f} tokens/s (first token after {first - start:.2f} s)") EOF It ends with a line like 5142 tokens at 1,717 tokens/s (first token after 0.04 s) . We see 1,700-1,770 tokens/s on 4xGB300 and 1,980-2,170 tokens/s on 8xB300 ( --gpus 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ). The server's request_end log line reports each request's step time ( average_iteration_ms ) and acceptance length
( average_accept_length ). Over 30 runs we see 3.24-3.37 ms and 5.1-6.1 tokens/step on 4xGB300, and 2.69-2.74 ms and
5.3-6.1 tokens/step on 8xB300. title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live
abstract:
PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live In July, we announced a series of planned updates to the PyPI user interface. Shaped by user research with members of the Python community , the updates aim to improve how we surface security signals and display package details. We're pleased to share that this work is now complete and live on PyPI . Context ¶ With the rapid growth of the Python ecosystem, PyPI has become an increasingly attractive target for malicious actors. In response, the PyPI team has delivered many security features while taking a more active role in helping PyPI users assess and understand package security. Digital attestations , introduced in 2024, are an example of this effort, providing a verifiable record of a release file's provenance (where it came from). However, provenance and attestations are still unfamiliar concepts for many PyPI users, and PyPI's interface did little to communicate their meaning, importance, or limitations. To address this, PyPI partnered with Kabu Creative to bring clearer security signals to the PyPI UI, implementing the recommendations developed in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide . Here's a look at what's changed, what it means for you, and what actions you can take. The New Security Tab ¶ The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from. The new security tab on a PyPI project detail page Provenance States ¶ PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation. Typically, a release will be in one of two states: Full Provenance ¶ This means that 100% of the release files have attestations, carrying either or both of the supported attestation types: PyPI Publish attestations confirm the file was published by a PyPI Trusted Publisher : A PyPI Publish attestation on PyPI SLSA Build Provenance attestations link the file back to its exact source commit, build platform, and instructions: A SLSA Build Provenance attestation on PyPI You can review attestation metadata directly in the UI, or click on the transparency log link for more information. No Provenance ¶ "No provenance" simply means that no file in the release has an attestation. This is typical for older releases or projects that have not yet configured Trusted Publishing. No provenance does not necessarily indicate that a release or release file is malicious; it instead means that the file origin cannot be cryptographically verified . When there is no provenance, you should rely on surrounding trust signals to assess security, such as maintainer history, release patterns, and repository activity. If you maintain the package, consider using Trusted Publishing with a publisher that generates attestations for your next release. Provenance Warnings ¶ Provenance warnings are designed to help you identify when a file may not have come from the project's maintainers, for example, if an attacker has taken over an account or a publishing workflow. When provenance metadata looks unusual or conflicts with a project's history, PyPI surfaces a prominent warning. Many warnings have legitimate explanations, but each one is worth checking before you install. Incomplete Provenance ¶ This means that some files carry attestations while others do not (e.g., wheels were published via Trusted Publishing, but the source tarball was uploaded using an API token). Exercise caution if you see this warning. Check release notes for build issues or ask in the project's issue tracker before installing. Inconsistent Provenance ¶ This warning indicates that files within the same release originate from different build systems or source repositories. Check the attestation metadata to confirm whether all files came from sources controlled by the maintainers. Change of Provenance ¶ This warning tells you that the release files originated from a different repository or workflow than a previous release. While often legitimate (such as an organization name change or repository migration), it can also indicate a compromised pipeline or account takeover. If you see this warning, check the project release notes or official channels to confirm that an infrastructure migration was planned. Loss of Provenance ¶ This means that a project that previously published with attestations has changed to uploading release files without them. Check whether the maintainers intentionally changed their publishing process, for example by switching back to API tokens, or by changing their publishing configuration so that it no longer generates attestations. If this is unexpected, treat the release with skepticism until verified. To learn more about provenance and attestations, including provenance warnings, see our user documentation . An example provenance warning on PyPI, showing a release with incomplete provenance Redesigned Project Detail Page ¶ To support these changes, the project detail page has also been updated: Provenance warnings now appear at the top of the page, alongside status banners for yanked releases, archived projects, and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined , only the quarantine banner is shown, as it takes precedence over all other warnings and banners. When a release has full provenance or provenance warnings, its provenance state is displayed in the sidebar, linking through to the security tab for more information. Metadata is now ordered by utility and labeled as "PyPI data" or "Data verified by PyPI", replacing the old design where data was grouped and ordered by verification status. The redesigned metadata sidebar, with information ordered by utility Release Files and Release History ¶ The redesigned release files tab helps you find the right file by searching and filtering long lists. You can also view the provenance state of each file within the table, and quickly identify late files, which are marked with an orange warning icon. Late file warnings are shown when one or more files were uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release timestamp. These warnings only appear on releases prior to July 2026, when a policy was introduced to reject new files after 14 days . The release history tab now also provides more details about each release, exposing file count, provenance state, and release status (i.e., quarantined, yanked, archived, or pre-release). The redesigned release history tab, with release status, file count, and provenance state Getting Help ¶ Alongside the interface updates, PyPI's user documentation has been extended to help you better navigate package security. Read our package security guide to learn about: Assessing source code security Checking provenance (where a package came from) Verifying package integrity Protecting yourself from common security attacks Reporting security issues Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments ¶ The new security tab gives PyPI a dedicated home for future attestation types and security notices. To help the wider open source ecosystem benefit from this work, we've also published a case study in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide detailing the design patterns and warnings developed during this project. This initiative was funded by the Open Source Security Foundation and implemented by Kabu Creative . We would like to thank Dustin Ingram , Zach Steindler , and the members of the OpenSSF Securing Software Repositories Working Group for championing this effort. Special thanks to Mike Fiedler , Jacob Coffee , and members of the PyPI team for their thoughtful design feedback and code reviews, @cofiem for their contributions to the new release files tab, and our user interview participants and community testers for helping shape the final design. Finally, we would like to thank the OpenSSF for its funding and continued partnership in securing the Python packaging ecosystem.

title: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots
abstract:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams. The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it. OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen. OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022. OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world. The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots. Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks. Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, reacted to the change at OpenAI, telling Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work. OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works. But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models. The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027. This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own. But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said. Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard. Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said. Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection. “There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run. For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots. Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former members of the once-unified, stand-alone OpenAI robotics team milled about. They still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. After all, one of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable—and the experience of those former OpenAI robotics researchers, now dispatched to other teams, offered one answer. title: The Claude Delusion
abstract:
Something weird happens to people who are successful. They start to think they're gods. Actually accomplishing anything is obviously no strict pre-requisite of success. And maybe it's not so much "being successful", but rather "being rich". How do you become rich? Some people are just lucky. Lucky to have a physical talent, lucky to have parents able and willing to nurture your talent, and of course quite often lucky to have been at the right place at the right time 1 . Being lucky doesn't mean they didn't also work hard. But even—especially!—the Paris Hiltons of the world, the children of Hollywood superstars, the crooks starting their corrupt empires with " a small loan " (or a share of an emerald mine) from their fathers—they all strongly believe that they deserve their success and then conclude that anybody not as successful only has themselves to blame. This is especially the case for people in tech, where for years and years being good at programming has been equated with overall (and often: superior) intelligence 2 , and those illusory superiority effects then amplify rampant Dunning-Kruger to quickly turn " I am good at writing code, and with some luck, I managed to be successful " into a train of thought that goes more like " I am successful. Success is not random, so I must deserve my success. I appear to be a genius, I've mastered coding, anything else is trivial. Ergo, I am good at everything . " Let's take Bill Gates as an example. Now, mind you, Bill Gates certainly has accomplished a lot, and his skillset and professional background includes without a doubt a lot of computer programming and various ruthless monopolistic business tactics. In a recent New York Times interview , he describes how he evaluated OpenAI's level of progress (emphasis mine): Now Bill Gates surely has shown an interest in biology and, through his work with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, has probably read a lot of articles and research in this field. But the hubris to think himself a subject matter expert able to make up advanced, novel questions in a scientific field outside his own and suitable to assess AI's true capabilities and then being "shocked" that it could answer these questions makes my point. Although, what really cooks his noodle is the idea that AI can do what he used to do: write code. Take note of the emphasis I added: the very notion that something else could be " as good as I am " is, first of all, hard to believe and secondly necessarily means that it's " superhuman ". That man is not lacking self-esteem, no sirree, Bob. Likewise, this is also where many of the tech bros appear to be losing their minds , and this thinking ("Anything approaching my skill level is superhuman.") explains a lot about how we ended up with both stories of ultimate doom and human extinction as well as the utopian nirvana where AI solves all of mankind's problems (well, all of the billionaires' problems, which appear to largely converge on pesky mortality ). For most tech nerds, being good at programming computers was a differentiating skill. It was weird, normies didn't understand it at all, you spoke your own language (languages!), you could make a computer do things . You understood how the internet works, and anything that's not working was clearly written by complete and utter morons, and you could easily write this yourself in an afternoon if you wanted to. So now you've created a computer program that can do the same thing. Your mind boggles! And it speaks! It confirms you, it praises you, it tells you that you're brilliant—clearly evidence that it is infallible itself. But now imagine if it was better than you. What at first seems inconceivable then must strike fear and awe in your heart, for you have created a powerful monster with direction and purpose all its own . (And you sure have consumed enough pulpy science fiction to know that your creature is coming for you eventually.) "Can you imagine a Beowulf cluster of these?" was an old Slashdot meme before memes were a thing. But the notion of having an army of minions to do your bidding has always appealed to the nerds looking to assert their superiority, and thus we arrived at "agents". "Swarms" of "autonomous" "agents". This narrative of agency conveniently also relieves you of responsibility. You didn't fail to properly restrict a potentially malicious program you trained to hack other systems with persistence. No, the "agents" went "rogue". You have summoned powerful daemons indeed. Daemons that can produce code faster than you (gasp!), code you don't fully understand (although of course you could, you just don't want to, you don't have time, you have too much going on, what with your homegrown heavily customized harness). It becomes obvious quite quickly that this, then, must be SUPERINTELLIGENCE. Superintelligence that COULD KILL US ALL! I picked on Bill Gates above to illustrate the overconfidence effect , but of course there is no shortage of much more exaggerated egos making bold statements outside of (or even within ) their purported area of expertise, reflecting a complete and utter inability to relate to other people. To them, we're all just NPCs . The more powerful people are, the less empathy they exhibit. This is neither news nor limited to tech; dog knows there are countless rich assholes outside of tech doing asshole things . But few outside the tech sector suffer the same level of delusion, of thinking themselves solely and uniquely qualified to decide mankind's future, to claim to have birthed a digital Prometheus, to boldly declare (and use as a perpetual shield) a literal Deus ex Machina to cure all diseases —if only they could find the time to prioritize that sort of work over, say, their military contracts . Pretending to even remotely care about climate change 3 while at the same time undoing " 15 years' worth of greenhouse gas reductions " and then listing environmental concerns as a risk factor in your S1 is just the cherry on top. If these are the new American Gods... well, je n'ai jamais eu besoin de cette hypothèse-là . [1] The actual citation for " Bill Gates went to one of the only high schools in the world that had a computer " is " The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel; Malcolm Gladwell discusses this in Outliers as well. ↩ [2] The entire interview circus in the tech world revolved around this notion of exclusivity and brilliant jerks: " Google hires geniuses " was an oft-repeated mantra in Silicon Valley, so logically, if you were hired by Google, you were a genius. (Yes, all >180,000 of Google's employees.) This translates to the other big or exclusive companies, and explains why everybody leaving will always note that they were always surrounded by the most brilliant minds. It's Inverse Groucho Marx Bias . ↩ [3] And hey, we really don't need AI to "figure out how to combat climate change". We already know how to do it. We just have to actually show any willingness to stop it. Unfortunately, that's also exactly where these megalomaniacs get in the way. ↩

title: Characterizing and Detecting Bugs at the Interfaces of OpenBSD Privilege-Separated Programs
abstract: Compartmentalization is an approach that limits the amount of damage a bug or security breach can wreak by decomposing a program into isolated compartments that each run with the least degree of privilege necessary. When compartmentalizing a program, developers must carefully harden the communications between compartments (i.e., compartment interfaces) to prevent attacks from spreading across boundaries. Unfortunately, this hardening is error-prone and often ad-hoc, leading to Compartment Interface Vulnerabilities (CIVs), a class of bugs that can render compartmentalized programs no more secure than their monolithic counterparts. Despite the potential impact of these bugs, the community has little understanding of how effective today's interface defenses are. This work systematically evaluates the strengths and limitations of CIV defenses deployed in production-grade compartmentalized programs. We audit a representative corpus of 25 popular compartmentalized programs in OpenBSD using a combination of manual analysis, fuzzing, and LLM agents. Our study identifies 81 CIVs, some over a decade old, with impacts as varied as memory corruption, information leakage, and logic bugs, and as severe as arbitrary code execution. We systematize our findings to extract high-level patterns that characterize these issues and derive more effective approaches to address them. Our results expose the strengths of OpenBSD's approach, such as how its avoidance of shared memory eliminates entire classes of issues. However, we also show that even programs compartmentalized by security experts remain vulnerable to recurring, high-impact CIV patterns. At the core, these findings highlight the need for clear (and ideally formal) specifications of compartment interfaces to achieve systematic counter-measures. This paper demonstrates flaws in existing compartmentalization schemes and provides a foundation for future work on the discovery and mitigation of CIVs.

title: LEASH: Zero-Trust Containment for AI Agent Swarms
abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly spawn sub-agent swarms that carry derived credentials to APIs, databases, and production infrastructure. When an operator kills a misbehaving orchestrator, its descendants keep exercising valid credentials for minutes to hours, since every deployed revocation mechanism needs network connectivity to a central authority, unavailable precisely when the network is degraded or adversarial. This paper presents LEASH - Liveness-Enforced Authorization for Swarm Hierarchies, which applies the zero-trust principle of continuous verification to a delegation hierarchy without a reachable authority. A parent emits a signed, epoch-indexed liveness beacon every Δh seconds, where Δh is the beacon interval, and each child staples a fresh beacon into every authentication proof, and the enforcement point checks freshness using only cached public keys and a local clock. Revocation happens by omission: when beacons stop, all descendants fail closed within a bounded zombie window Wz ≤ Wmax  + Δh + ϵ , where Wmax  is the maximum beacon age and ϵ is the clock skew. Immediate-parent verification at O(1) and full-chain verification at O(d), where d is the hierarchy depth, extend this bound against compromised intermediates. We evaluate LEASH with real GPT-4o-mini agent swarms: 0.71% tool-call overhead, cascading revocation across a 49-agent four-level hierarchy within bound, and 295 × less credential-theft exposure versus OAuth 2.0. Under prompt injection that bypasses application-layer guardrails, LEASH denies every post-revocation tool call, since enforcement sits below the LLM.

title: SymSan: Mitigating Malware Embedding in Large Language Models via Parameter Space Symmetry
abstract: Despite the considerable advantages of open-source large language models (LLMs) in terms of interpretability and customizability, the full-access sharing paradigm inevitably exposes them to a severe security threat, i.e., malware embedding attacks (MEAs), where adversaries embed malware binaries (i.e., payloads) into model parameters for subsequent execution. While existing sanitization defenses have been explored to eliminate payloads within parameters, they exhibit limited generalization against emerging MEAs and lack theoretical guarantees for model utility preservation. In this paper, we propose SymSan, an effective LLM sanitization method grounded in parameter space symmetry theory. SymSan leverages rigorously designed permutation and scaling symmetries, systematically transforming parameter matrices across complementary component pairs, thereby eliminating embedded payloads while ensuring mathematical functional equivalence. Experiments across diverse LLMs against a wide spectrum of MEAs demonstrate that SymSan achieves at least 0.47 BER against all evaluated existing MEAs while maintaining equivalent model performance on both foundational and downstream tasks, significantly outperforming all baselines.

title: Improving Transparency and Accountability in AI Data Use
abstract: The rise of generative AI has rapidly increased the amount of data needed to both train models and ground generated responses with updated factual information. These needs are particularly relevant to AI-based chatbots. Developers of such systems initially gather training data to teach models how to generate new content, then provide deployed models with tools to reference information online (''real-time content retrieval'') to ensure content generated is up to date. However, implementation details of this data acquisition often remain unknown. This dissertation seeks to understand how AI models - specifically proprietary AI chatbots - ingest and process content from the web. The long-term goal of this research is to increase the control people have over how their online content is used in AI models. Our research will do this by unveiling details of existing data use methodologies in AI systems and creating new tools to control such data use. Thus far our research has revealed that AI chatbots acquire data from websites in unexpected ways, spoofing as human visitors or scraping data from third parties. Future work will perform additional measurement studies of generative AI systems and develop new tools to give web hosts greater control over their data.

title: Time Will Tell: Illuminating Causes of Score Inflation in Source Code Vulnerability Detection Benchmarks
abstract: LLM-based source code vulnerability detection (SCVD) reports strong benchmark performance that does not hold up in the real world. Use of random splitting in test-set construction has been widely blamed for permitting time-travel and inter-commit leakage, but neither mechanism has been empirically isolated. We evaluate five different cross-validation strategies across eight fine-tuned and eight zero-shot LLMs on MegaVul-C; every strategy is also evaluated on the same held-out future set to separate training-set from test-set effects. Random splitting inflates reported test-set F1 by ∼ 34% for fine-tuned models and ∼ 16% for zero-shot models. On the shared holdout set, models fine-tuned using random and temporal training splits achieve statistically equivalent performance within ± 2 pp (pTOST < 0.001), which places the inflation on test-set construction. Matched comparisons that isolate inter-commit leakage and time-travel are equivalent on the holdout set within the same margin. Correcting the train-test CWE distribution by resampling, our proxy for evolving vulnerability patterns, does not close the gap either. The gap instead reflects differences between the training and evaluation distributions, which we localize but do not reduce to a single causal property. Temporal splitting remains necessary for realistic evaluation because it reduces the optimistic bias of random test-set construction. We recommend Temporal LOO Block CV, which preserves the variance reduction of K-fold evaluation while inducing distribution shift at each fold boundary. All split-generation, analysis, and training code is released to support reproducible evaluation of LLMs for SCVD.

title: Governing AI Agent with Capability and Delegation Chain
abstract: As LLM-based agents move from personal productivity assistants to enterprise workflow executors, security requirements shift from controlling model outputs to governing real-world decisions and tool invocations. Existing defenses improve robustness, but still struggle to enforce fine-grained, verifiable authority continuously across multi-hop delegation in autonomous workflows. We present CapAgent, an access-control and identity-delegation framework for AI agents that combines capability-constrained credentials with delegation-chain semantics. In CapAgent, authority is encoded as cryptographically protected, derivable credentials with explicit API/parameter constraints, lifecycle rules, and cross-hop provenance. CapAgent couples a protocol for issuance, derivation, verification, and auditing with a three-layer architecture, and we implement it as a layered SDK with CLI and MCP integration, together with a multi-agent governance prototype for intent compilation. Our evaluation includes symbolic verification, enforcement case studies of out-of-scope actions, public agent-security benchmarks (ASB and AgentDojo), and performance measurements of core operations. Results indicate that CapAgent achieves least-privilege multi-hop delegation with practical near-local overhead, supporting production-grade autonomous agent operations.

title: Out of Tune: How Different Fine-Tuning Methods Affect Information Security
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) enables task specialization but introduces privacy risks through training data memorization. Practitioners deploying fine-tuned LLMs in sensitive domains such as medicine, law, and finance must choose among fine-tuning methods without clear guidance on the privacy implications of that choice. We compare full fine-tuning, partial fine-tuning, and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by measuring how much sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) each method leaks from training data, using planted canaries to track memorization. Six Llama configurations (3B and 8B parameters) are evaluated across the medical, legal, and finance domains under three extraction attack types: prefix attacks, random prompting, and completion attacks. Full fine-tuning leaks the most on average, followed by LoRA. Partial fine-tuning leaks the least in every configuration we tested, though the relative ordering of full fine-tuning and LoRA varies. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, LoRA's parameter efficiency does not yield the strongest privacy protection; we attribute this to LoRA's architectural breadth across all transformer layers. The performance-privacy trade-off these findings expose has direct consequences for deployment. Even partial fine-tuning on the 3B model, our best configuration, leaked canaries, so practitioners should assume some leakage by default.

title: Emergence-Driven Security of LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer limited to text generators, but they can also plan, call tools, delegate tasks to other agents, act within external environments, and change states in response to their actions. In Anthropic’s recent report on an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign involving Claude Code, individual subtasks appeared legitimate when evaluated in isolation but became malicious when combined into an autonomous attack sequence. Consequently, the security of such complex LLM-based agentic systems may fail even when each component appears secure in isolation. This position and open-problem paper argues that LLM agent security should be studied as emergence-driven security: the analysis of security properties that arise from the interactions among agents and its components over time. We define emergence-driven security and provide a conceptual taxonomy to classify emergent security-related phenomena in LLM agents, covering both beneficial and harmful forms of emergence. Based on these insights, we propose EASE, an Emergence-Aware Security Evaluation framework that provides a systematic process for assessing how interactions among agents combine over time to produce harmful or beneficial system-level security outcomes. Finally, we conclude by outlining open problems for studying emergent behavior in LLM agents in the context of security. The paper is intended to provide a foundation for examining how the emerging capabilities and operational needs of LLM agents may shape security evaluations that go beyond static, model-level testing.

title: ArchProof: A Sound Output-Contribution Certificate for Dormant-Gate Path Backdoors in ONNX Models
abstract: Architectural backdoors are malicious subgraphs hard-wired into a neural network's computational graph. They survive weight-based defenses and are flagged by commercial scanners as a first-class threat to ONNX deployment. Existing detection relies on heuristic signatures or probabilistic sampling; a sound deterministic quantitative certificate for any formally defined subclass of this threat is missing. We present ArchProof, a verifier that reads an ONNX model and a clean-input calibration set and returns a sound output-contribution ε-certificate over a decidable class of additive dormant-gate path backdoors. The certificate is a worst-case bound, not an estimate of what a trigger does to the output. Its use is threefold: a one-sided verdict, a per-gate ranking, and a bound that reaches zero once the flagged gates are removed. Three theorems then bound how the certificate behaves under deployment stress: it degrades within bounds when the calibration set is poisoned, a greedy algorithm finds the smallest set of gates to remove for any target level, and it stays stable across semantics-preserving ONNX exports. We evaluate on production CNN, transformer-encoder, and decoder-only LLM ONNX graphs against heuristic and ablation baselines.

title: SpecStega: Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography Based on Speculative Sampling in Asymmetric Resource Scenarios
abstract: Provably secure generative steganography embeds secret messages by guiding the sampling process of a Language Model (LM) without altering its original probability distribution. Existing methods typically rely on a strict white-box assumption, requiring both the sender and receiver to share an identical LM. To ensure the linguistic fluency necessary to avoid abnormal behavior, the shared model is usually a large LM. However, this assumption is often impractical in asymmetric resource scenarios where receivers are constrained to resource-limited edge devices (e.g., mobile phones) capable of running only a small LM. This computational discrepancy creates a covertness dilemma between achieving high-quality stego text generation and ensuring efficient decodability. While existing black-box methods attempt to bypass model access for decoding, they fail to fully leverage the receiver's available resources, resulting in limited payload capacity. To resolve this dilemma, we propose a novel gray-box steganography, SpecStega, that utilizes the shared draft small LM for message embedding to ensure receiver compatibility, while leveraging speculative sampling with the target large LM to refine the output. This ensures that the final stego text aligns with the target LM's distribution, preserving high-quality linguistic fluency and security. To mitigate decoding errors caused by the distribution mismatch between the target and draft LMs, we introduce a robust decoding mechanism based on evidence accumulation and noise suppression. Experimental results demonstrate that SpecStega increases payload capacity by over 20x compared to the existing black-box solution in asymmetric resource scenarios. Our method successfully bridges a critical gap in practical steganography, achieving the high-quality stego text generated by the target LM while maintaining efficient decodability via the draft LM.

title: 11th Workshop on Traffic Measurements for Cybersecurity (WTMC)
abstract: The Workshop on Traffic Measurements for Cybersecurity (WTMC) provides a forum for research grounded in traffic measurements and empirical observations of security-relevant online phenomena. WTMC brings together researchers and practitioners from academia and industry to examine how measurements of network traffic, protocols, applications, platforms, and Internet-scale infrastructure can improve our understanding of cyberattacks, online abuse, defensive mechanisms, and their operational impact. The workshop welcomes original research, measurement methodologies, empirical studies, operational experience, and reappraisals of previous findings. Its scope includes malware, botnets, phishing, network anomalies, abuse infrastructures, attack detection and mitigation, the economics of cybersecurity, and the emerging role of generative AI in cyberattacks and defense.

title: Embodied AI Must Treat Visual Bias as a Safety Primitive, Not a Robustness Penalty
abstract: While embodied agents increasingly incorporate diverse sensors, they predominantly rely on learned visual representations for manipulation and control. However, when visual preferences are tightly coupled with action generation, benign cues can induce task failures, unsafe motions, or exploitable vulnerabilities. We present a diagnostic study of visual bias as a safety primitive for embodied AI evaluation and defense: an independently operationalizable property tied to an identifiable risk class, not a standalone safety guarantee. Agents should be assessed not merely on task success, but also on whether their actions remain grounded in visual evidence relevant to the task. We study this risk through controlled visual variations under task-equivalent conditions, naturalistic distractors aligned with inherited visual preferences, and counterfactual action analysis. Our results show that benign perceptual changes can produce divergent behavior, while task-irrelevant content can receive disproportionate action relevance and induce physical failures. We further introduce a counterfactual detection method that combines persistent region selection with changes in predicted actions after masking, helping distinguish behaviorally relevant preference-aligned content from regions that are merely visually salient. These findings provide preliminary diagnostic evidence of visual bias and demonstrate the need for broader preference discovery, visual shortcut mining, and failure mode search to improve predeployment risk coverage and guide targeted mitigation in both model development and real-world deployment.

title: Code-SeC: A Decoding-time Probing Method for Characterizing Secret Memorization in Code LLM
abstract: Code Large Language Models (Code LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in code generation and completion. While these models are known to memorize portions of their training data, existing approaches to evaluate credential memorization rely on output-level inspection or adversarial prompt crafting, leaving the internal decoding behaviors that underlie secret leakage unexplored. In this paper, we conduct a token-level investigation of hard-coded credential memorization in Code LLMs during routine code completion. We report two findings: (1) traces of memorized secrets persist in the token candidate space, indicating that standard output-level evaluation underestimates the true extent of memorization; (2) the generation of real secrets exhibits statistically distinct uncertainty dynamics compared to hallucinated strings, providing a reliable intrinsic signal for memorization detection. Based on these findings, we propose Code-SeC (Code Secret Characterization), a decoding-time diagnostic framework that monitors uncertainty signals along the decoding trajectory and performs targeted distribution adjustments to uncover latent credential memorization. Experimental results show that Code-SeC effectively detects memorized code secrets across representative Code LLMs and secret types, providing comprehensive empirical evidence that hard-coded credential memorization is prevalent in current code completion models.

title: Reverse Prompt Engineering in Generative AI: A Baseline for Deepfake, Deception and Disinformation Mitigation
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has democratised content creation while scaling systemic threats in Deepfakes, Deception, and Disinformation (D3). As traditional content detection and watermarking are increasingly bypassed, this paper presents a position and baseline synthesis of Reverse Prompt Engineering (RPE) as a defensive capability. RPE inverts the generative pipeline to infer plausible instruction prompts and support, rather than definitively proving source-model attribution. Grounded in threat telemetry, we synthesise representative RPE frameworks while explicitly delineating the evidentiary limits of prompt recovery, attribution, and content provenance. We further evaluate RPE across public information, legal, and policy/governance viewpoints, analyse key technical limitations such as cross-modal generalisation, and outline a research roadmap to establish RPE as a cornerstone of digital provenance and AI accountability.

title: Does AI Amplify Online Hate- A Multi-Modal Measurement Study on 4chan's /pol/
abstract: As generative AI models gain widespread adoption, an urgent question arises: are they being exploited to produce hateful content in online communities? We present the first large-scale, multi-modal measurement study to investigate this question, drawing on 465M text posts spanning 2016-2026 and 16.9M images spanning 2021-2025 from 4chan's /pol/ board. Specifically, we focused on two hate targets with long-established phenomena in parallel: anti-Indian hate and anti-Semitic hate. By benchmarking five text and five image AI detectors on hateful content, we deploy the best-performing detectors on over 31K long-form hateful posts and approximately 50K hateful images to measure AI-generated content prevalence. We find that the two targets exhibit different growth patterns: anti-Indian hate is substantially self-sustaining, with 46.15% of detected peaks driven by organized community campaigns rather than external events, against only 5.88% for anti-Semitic hate, which is instead largely reactive, with 94.12% of peaks triggered by real-world events such as the October 7 Hamas attack. AI-generated hateful posts have grown steadily since late 2022, reaching 1.42% of long-form posts by 2025. More importantly, AI adoption diverges across the two targets. For anti-Indian hate, AI content prevalence correlates significantly with slur frequency, nearly doubles during hate peaks, and AI-generated posts are 55.72% more toxic than human-written ones. Anti-Semitic hate, by contrast, shows no significant AI-hate correlation, indicating that AI tools are more widely adopted in campaign-driven hate than in established hate discourse. Lead-lag analysis reveals that hate campaigns precede AI adoption by approximately three months, suggesting that generative AI serves as an accelerator for existing hate movements rather than an independent driver.

title: Secrecy in Squirrel and the Post-Compromise Security of a Ratchet
abstract: Ratchets are critical cryptographic protocols deployed in many secure messaging applications such as Signal Messenger, WhatsApp, and Apple's iMessage PQ3, which aim for strong guarantees such as Post-Compromise Security (PCS). Computer-aided cryptography can be used to increase confidence in security protocols but, until now, has been unable to prove PCS in the computational model for a ratchet due to the complexity of the cryptographic arguments involved. Existing mechanized PCS analyses have been limited to the symbolic model. We tackle this problem with Squirrel, which is well-suited to study such stateful protocols. The task is still a challenge, due to the intricate reasoning required, and because Squirrel's indirect modeling of secrecy has difficulties in scaling to such a complex proof. To address these issues, we develop a novel logical framework in Squirrel that allows to reason on secrecy as a first-class notion, and we validate our approach by verifying the PCS of an asymmetric ratchet. This provides the first mechanized computational proof of PCS to date for a ratchet, and possibly for any protocol.

title: POSTER: UniAlert: Cost-Efficient Unified Representation of Multi-Source Heterogeneous Alert Logs with LLMs
abstract: Multi-zone IDS deployments improve detection coverage but also introduce large volumes of heterogeneous alerts generated by diverse IDS platforms. Existing alert denoising methods are not readily applicable to such alerts, as they typically assume a unified schema and consistent field semantics. Alert normalization approaches partially mitigate this issue by leveraging manually crafted prior knowledge. However, constructing and maintaining such knowledge requires substantial expert effort and limits their adaptability to evolving log schemas. To address these challenges, we present UniAlert, an LLM-based system for accurate and cost-efficient unified representation of alert logs. UniAlert extracts field-level context from log trees to constrain LLM reasoning and improve field mapping accuracy. It further uses incremental field-mapping templates and selectively invokes LLMs only for unseen log formats or template updates, significantly reducing token cost. Preliminary results show that, compared with state-of-the-art methods, UniAlert improves field-mapping F1 by 20.06%-57.78% while reducing token consumption by 98.69% compared with LLM-only.

title: Accio: Detecting Privilege Escalation Vulnerabilities in DBMSs via Minimum Privilege Set Calculation
abstract: Access control mechanisms in DBMSs enforce user privileges for executing SQL operations. They are critical for protecting the confidentiality and integrity of stored data. However, implementation errors can lead to privilege escalation, allowing unauthorized actions that appear legitimate to the system. We refer to such errors as privilege escalation vulnerabilities (PEVs), which can result in severe consequences, including denial of service, data leakage, and data tampering. Despite their serious impact, the characteristics of PEVs remain largely unexplored, and systematic detection methods are still lacking. In this paper, we present a motivation study of 63 real-world privilege escalation cases from 5 widely used DBMSs. Our analysis shows that many vulnerabilities stem from missing privilege checks, incorrect privilege resolution, or operation-privilege mismatches. Detecting these PEVs requires careful reasoning about the interactions between SQL operations, user privileges, and execution contexts. Guided by these insights, we design and implement Accio, which detects privilege escalation vulnerabilities via minimum privilege set calculation. It models privilege hierarchies, computes the minimum set of privileges required for each SQL command, and checks consistency against expected policies. We evaluated Accio on seven widely used DBMSs, discovering 26 previously unknown PEVs, all confirmed, and 23 of which have been fixed. Accio also successfully detects historical privilege escalation cases and has been positively recognized by developers for its practical impact.

title: zkTransformer: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for LLM Inference via Einsum Arithmetization and Structured Exponentiation Lookups
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed through cloud APIs; however, their inference processes are opaque and cannot be externally audited without revealing proprietary model parameters. Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) enable verifiable inference while preserving model confidentiality, but existing zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) systems remain difficult to deploy in practice due to limitations in developer usability, completeness of prover implementations, and the cost of lookup operations. We present \zkt, an end-to-end zkML framework for transformer inference that addresses these challenges while achieving high prover performance. To improve usability and correctness, we introduce \zkes, a new sumcheck-based arithmetization that lifts linear tensor operations to an AI-friendly abstraction based on Einstein summation (Einsum), enabling automatic compilation of such operations into a single Sumcheck instance without manual circuit engineering over low-level addition and multiplication gates. To reduce the cost of nonlinear operations, we further propose \zkexp, a structured lookup technique for exponentiation that eliminates the need for table-sized commitments. Together, these techniques provide a unified and model-agnostic framework for verifiable transformer inference, supporting standard architectures such as GPT-2 and LLaMA2-7B. We implement and open-source \zkt. On GPT-2, it achieves an amortized prover time of 3.4 seconds per token, representing a 5--10× speedup over state-of-the-art systems such as zkLLM and zkGPT.

title: Global-View Reasoning with LLMs for Real-World Vulnerability Detection
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in code generation and other software engineering tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world security vulnerability detection still remains limited. A key observation is that while LLMs exhibit strong semantic understanding and security analysis capabilities on code snippets, these strengths are rarely extended to large-scale real-world programs. In this work, we propose SemScan, a novel vulnerability detection approach that harnesses LLMs' local reasoning capabilities to enable global security analysis. SemScan establishes an iterative loop of evidence collection and evidence-guided semantic synthesis. Our evaluation on a Python CVE vulnerability dataset and 200 popular real-world Python projects demonstrates that SemScan significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tools, uncovering 62 previously unknown serious vulnerabilities, including remote code execution and insecure deserialization flaws. To date, 22 of these vulnerabilities have been confirmed and assigned CVE identifiers.
